pillar: Other dimensions & the physics of reality

lines.say: Fire tiny particles, like electrons, one at a time at a wall with two narrow slits. Behind it, a screen records where each one lands.
shots: line art: electron gun, two slits, screen

lines.say: Each electron hits the screen as a single dot. But after thousands, the dots form stripes, an interference pattern. The kind waves make when they pass through both slits at once.
shots: line art: dots accumulating into stripes
q: water ripples interfering two sources

lines.say: In 1989, a team at Hitachi filmed exactly this, electron by electron.
shots: line art: stripes building up time-lapse

lines.say: Now add a detector to see which slit each electron goes through. The stripes vanish. You get two plain bands, like particles.
shots: line art: detector at slit, two bands

lines.say: This is where the internet says: consciousness changes reality. That's not what physicists mean by observing.
shots: line art: eye icon crossed out

lines.say: Observing means any interaction that records which path the particle took. A machine does it. No human needs to look.
shots: line art: detector records path, no person

lines.say: What it really means for reality is still debated. But the experiment is real, and it's one of the strangest things we know.

fact_note: Double-slit with single electrons, Tonomura et al., Hitachi 1989 (KNOWN). Which-path detection destroys interference (KNOWN). 'Observation' = measurement/decoherence, not consciousness (KNOWN mainstream; interpretations of QM DEBATED).
ig_caption: the double slit is real and it's insane, but 'your mind changes reality' is not what it shows. took me years to get that
tt_caption: the double slit experiment explained without the myths #quantumphysics #physics

pillar: Other dimensions & the physics of reality

lines.say: In 1884, a schoolteacher named Edwin Abbott published a novel about a world that's completely flat. It's called Flatland.
shots: line art: flat plane with shapes

lines.say: Its hero is a square. He can move forward, back, left and right. Up doesn't exist for him.
shots: line art: square moving on plane

lines.say: One day a sphere passes through his world. What does the square see? A dot appears from nowhere, grows into a circle, shrinks, and vanishes.
shots: line art: sphere passing through plane, circle growing / shrinking
q: ball descending into water surface

lines.say: The sphere lifts him out, and he sees his whole world from above, even the insides of houses, and of people.
shots: line art: plane seen from above, insides visible

lines.say: Now apply that to us. If a four-dimensional being passed through our world, we'd see a 3D object appear from nowhere, change size and shape, and vanish.
shots: line art: 3D blob appearing and changing

lines.say: It could see inside sealed rooms. Inside you. Without opening anything.
shots: line art: closed box with contents visible

lines.say: We have no evidence such beings exist. But mathematically, that's exactly what it would look like.
shots: q: starfield with geometric overlay phi

fact_note: Edwin A. Abbott, 'Flatland: A Romance of Many Dimensions', 1884 (KNOWN). Sphere's cross-section analogy (KNOWN math). Existence of 4D beings is SPECULATION; the cross-section logic is standard geometry.
ig_caption: this 1884 book about a square explains the 4th dimension better than anything I learned in school
tt_caption: Flatland and what a 4th dimension would look like #4thdimension #physics

pillar: Other dimensions & the physics of reality

lines.say: In 2003, an Oxford philosopher named Nick Bostrom published a short argument that still bothers people.
He said: imagine a civilization that gets powerful enough to simulate whole worlds, with conscious minds inside.
If they do that even a little, simulated minds would vastly outnumber real ones.
shots: line art: one real world, thousands of copies

lines.say: So one of three things must be true. One: almost every civilization dies before it gets that powerful.
Two: the ones that make it aren't interested in running simulations of their past.
Three: we are almost certainly living in one.
He never said which one is true. But if you reject the third, you have to accept one of the first two. And neither is very comforting.
shots: line art: three options, none chosen

fact_note: Bostrom, 'Are You Living in a Computer Simulation?', Philosophical Quarterly 2003 (KNOWN). Trilemma accurately stated (KNOWN). Bostrom doesn't claim we are in one (KNOWN). Conclusion is SPECULATION.
ig_caption: it's not 'we're in a simulation'. it's 'pick one of these three'. and all three are uncomfortable

pillar: Other dimensions & the physics of reality

lines.say: Every time your phone shows your location, it's correcting for Einstein's relativity. Here's how.
shots: q: phone map GPS location dot

lines.say: GPS satellites orbit about twenty thousand kilometers up, carrying very precise atomic clocks.
shots: archive: GPS satellite illustration (public domain, US gov)

lines.say: Because they move fast, special relativity says their clocks run slow, by about seven millionths of a second a day.
shots: line art: fast clock ticking slower

lines.say: But they're also farther from Earth's gravity, and general relativity says that makes clocks run faster, by about forty-five millionths a day.
shots: line art: gravity well, clock higher ticks faster

lines.say: Net result: they gain about thirty-eight microseconds every day.
Sounds tiny. But GPS works by timing signals at the speed of light. Left uncorrected, the error would grow by around ten kilometers a day.
shots: line art: map location drifting away

lines.say: So engineers tune the satellite clocks before launch. Time really does run differently up there, and your maps prove it every day.
shots: q: phone map in hand at night

fact_note: GPS altitude ~20,200 km (KNOWN). SR ~-7 us/day, GR ~+45 us/day, net ~+38 us/day (KNOWN). Uncorrected positional error ~10 km/day (KNOWN, commonly cited). Clock frequency offset set before launch (10.22999999543 MHz) (KNOWN).
ig_caption: GPS literally wouldn't work without Einstein. satellites age faster than us, by 38 microseconds a day
tt_caption: how GPS proves time dilation is real #relativity #physics

pillar: Other dimensions & the physics of reality
hook: They flew atomic clocks|*around the world*

lines.say: October 1971. Two scientists, Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating, buy plane tickets. Regular commercial flights. Around the world.
Their luggage: four atomic clocks, each one strapped into its own seat.
shots: line art: clock in airplane seat

lines.say: The question: does time pass differently if you move fast, or fly higher? Einstein said yes. Nobody had tested it with clocks on planes.
shots: line art: clock on ground vs clock in air

lines.say: They flew around the world eastward, then westward, and compared their clocks with the ones that stayed at the US Naval Observatory.
shots: line art: globe with eastward and westward arrows

lines.say: Flying east, the clocks lost about sixty billionths of a second. Flying west, they gained about two hundred and seventy.
Both results matched Einstein's predictions, within the experiment's margin of error.
shots: line art: predicted vs measured bars match

lines.say: Time literally ran at different speeds for the clocks on board. Two physicists proved it in economy class.

fact_note: Hafele-Keating experiment, Oct 1971, four cesium clocks on commercial flights (KNOWN). East: -59 +/- 10 ns; West: +273 +/- 7 ns vs USNO (KNOWN). Agreement with predictions within error (KNOWN). Clocks occupied seats (KNOWN, bought seats as 'Mr. Clock').
ig_caption: they bought plane seats for atomic clocks to test Einstein. and he was right
tt_caption: the Hafele Keating experiment, time dilation on airplanes #physics #einstein

pillar: Other dimensions & the physics of reality

lines.say: Quantum entanglement: two particles linked so that measuring one instantly tells you about the other, no matter how far apart they are.
shots: line art: two particles linked by line
q: two lights far apart in dark

lines.say: Einstein hated it. He called it spooky action at a distance, and argued in 1935 that quantum theory must be missing something.
In 1964, John Bell found a way to test it. Then, starting in the 1970s, experiments by John Clauser, Alain Aspect and Anton Zeilinger did.
Einstein lost. The correlations are real and stronger than any hidden local explanation allows. They won the Nobel Prize in 2022.
shots: line art: results beyond limit line

lines.say: Now the myth part. Entanglement does not let you send messages faster than light.
shots: line art: message crossed out between particles

lines.say: Each side alone just sees random results. You only see the link when you compare notes, and that comparison travels at normal speed.
shots: line art: two lists compared later

lines.say: So the universe really is connected in ways Einstein found unbearable. It just won't let you cheat with it.
shots: line art: thread between two points glowing

fact_note: EPR 1935 (KNOWN). 'Spooky action at a distance', letter to Born 1947 (KNOWN). Bell 1964 (KNOWN). Clauser 1972, Aspect 1982, Zeilinger; Nobel 2022 (KNOWN). No-signaling theorem (KNOWN).
ig_caption: the 'entanglement = instant communication' thing is everywhere and it's wrong. the real thing is weirder anyway
tt_caption: quantum entanglement explained, and the big myth #quantum #einstein

pillar: Other dimensions & the physics of reality

lines.say: Michele Besso was Einstein's closest friend. They met as students. Besso was the one person Einstein thanked in his 1905 paper on relativity.
They argued about physics and life for fifty years.
In March 1955, Besso died. Einstein, seventy-six and ill himself, wrote to Besso's family.
Now he has departed from this strange world a little ahead of me. That means nothing.
People like us, who believe in physics, know that the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion.
shots: line art: timeline with past / present / future fading

lines.say: In relativity, there's no single 'now' shared by the whole universe. Some physicists take that to mean all moments exist equally.
shots: q: film strip frames all visible

lines.say: Einstein died about a month later. He had already told us how he thought about it.

fact_note: Besso, acknowledged in 1905 SR paper (KNOWN). Besso died 15 March 1955; Einstein letter to the Besso family 21 March 1955 (KNOWN quote, standard translation). Einstein died 18 April 1955 (KNOWN). Relativity of simultaneity / block universe interpretation (KNOWN physics; metaphysical reading DEBATED).
ig_caption: the most beautiful thing Einstein ever wrote was a condolence letter. 'that means nothing'
tt_caption: Einstein's letter about time after his best friend died #einstein #time

pillar: Other dimensions & the physics of reality
hook: The physicist of parallel worlds|and the *rock star* son

lines.say: In 1957, a Princeton grad student named Hugh Everett proposed a wild solution to quantum physics.
In quantum theory, a particle can be in several possible states at once, until it's measured and seems to pick one. Everett said: what if it doesn't pick?
shots: line art: particle in superposition splitting

lines.say: Every possible outcome happens. Reality branches, again and again, into separate worlds that can't see each other.
Physicists mostly ignored it. Everett left academia, worked on defense computing, and died in 1982.
Years later, the many-worlds idea became one of the most discussed interpretations of quantum physics, defended by some leading physicists today.
shots: line art: many worlds branches glowing

lines.say: And his son became a musician: Mark Oliver Everett, frontman of the band Eels. He made a documentary trying to understand his father's physics.
If his father was right, there's a branch where Hugh Everett got to see the idea take off.

fact_note: Everett's relative-state formulation, 1957 (KNOWN). Initially neglected; worked at Pentagon WSEG / defense analysis (KNOWN). Died 1982 (KNOWN). Many-worlds now widely discussed (Deutsch, Carroll) (KNOWN). Son Mark Oliver Everett ('E') of Eels; BBC doc 'Parallel Worlds, Parallel Lives' 2007 (KNOWN). Many-worlds truth is SPECULATION/interpretation. Avoid other family details.
ig_caption: the guy who came up with parallel universes was ignored his whole life, and his son is the singer of Eels. didn't know this until last night
tt_caption: Hugh Everett, many worlds theory and his son from Eels #multiverse #quantum

pillar: Other dimensions & the physics of reality

lines.say: Let's zoom in. You, about a meter and a half.
A skin cell: a hundred thousand times smaller. Inside it, DNA. Then atoms, about a ten-billionth of a meter.
The nucleus of an atom: a hundred thousand times smaller again. If the atom were a stadium, the nucleus would be a pea in the middle.
shots: line art: pea at center of stadium

lines.say: Keep going. Twenty more steps of ten. You reach the Planck length, about point zero zero zero... thirty-four zeros, and then a one six, of a meter.
shots: line art: zeros counting across screen

lines.say: If an atom were blown up to the size of the observable universe, the Planck length would be roughly the height of a tree.
Below this scale, our physics stops making sense. And in string theory, this is where extra dimensions could hide, curled up too small to ever notice.
shots: line art: curled up dimension tubes

lines.say: Unproven, maybe untestable. But there may be more directions in space than the three you can point to.
shots: line art: 3 axes + faint extra axes

fact_note: Scales: cell ~10-30 um, atom ~1e-10 m, nucleus ~1e-15 m (KNOWN). Planck length 1.616e-35 m (KNOWN). Atom-to-universe comparison: 8.8e26/1e-10 = 8.8e36 x 1.6e-35 = ~14 m (computed; 'height of a tree'). String theory requires 10/11 dimensions, compactified (KNOWN theory; physical reality SPECULATION). 'Twenty more steps of ten' from 1e-15 to ~1e-35 (KNOWN).
ig_caption: if an atom were the size of the universe, the smallest possible length would be about as tall as a tree. my brain hurts
tt_caption: zooming down to the Planck length and hidden dimensions #physics #stringtheory

pillar: Other dimensions & the physics of reality

lines.say: Three experiments that show time doesn't work the way it feels.
One. Your head is aging faster than your feet. Gravity slows time. In 2010, physicists at NIST raised one atomic clock about a foot higher than another, and measured it ticking faster.
shots: line art: two clocks, one 33 cm higher
q: atomic clock lab NIST style

lines.say: Two. Speed slows time. Cosmic rays create particles called muons high in the atmosphere. They should decay long before reaching the ground.
shots: line art: muon decay timer running out

lines.say: They reach it anyway, in huge numbers. Moving at nearly the speed of light, their clocks run slow.
shots: line art: muon path to ground with slow clock

lines.say: Three. There's no universal now. Two events that happen at the same time for one observer can happen at different times for another, moving differently.
shots: line art: two observers, two flashes, different order

lines.say: Not one of these is a theory waiting for proof. They are measured, again and again.

fact_note: Chou et al., Science 2010, NIST optical clocks, 33 cm height difference (KNOWN). Muon survival via time dilation (KNOWN, Rossi-Hall 1941; Frisch-Smith 1963). Relativity of simultaneity (KNOWN; follows from SR, consistent with all tests).
ig_caption: your head is technically older than your feet. by a ridiculously small amount, but still
tt_caption: 3 experiments that prove time is relative #time #physics
